subtopic_detail: Fitness to drive on stimulant medication
stem:
A 34-year-old man is reviewed 8 weeks after commencing dexamfetamine sulfate 15 mg twice daily for newly diagnosed adult attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. He reports substantial improvement in workplace concentration and no cardiovascular symptoms. He is a private car driver only, does not hold a commercial licence, and has no history of previous crashes or driving offences. He asks whether he needs to notify the state driver licensing authority.

His blood pressure has been stable at 128/78 on treatment and his resting electrocardiogram remains normal. He has no history of substance use disorder and takes no other regular medications. He has not been advised by his psychiatrist to avoid driving. His partner and colleagues have commented that his concentration is much improved and he no longer misses turns or drifts across lanes on his commute.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 76, blood pressure 128/78, respiratory rate 14, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees
data_table.Investigations: resting ECG normal with sinus rhythm and QTc 400 milliseconds

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice regarding his driving?

options.text: He does not need to notify because his symptoms are well controlled on stimulant medication and he holds only a private not commercial licence class
options.rationale: Symptom control does not remove the notification obligation. ADHD remains a notifiable condition under Austroads and the state driver licensing authority determines the licence conditions. (Source: Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive 2022)
source_refs: Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive 2022

options.text: He must cease driving entirely because stimulant medications for ADHD disqualify all patients from holding an Australian driving licence permanently
options.rationale: Stimulant medication does not automatically disqualify a driver. Austroads assesses on the underlying condition and its treatment; most well-treated adults with ADHD retain their private licence with conditions. (Source: Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive 2022)
source_refs: Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive 2022

options.text: The doctor is required to notify the state driver licensing authority on the patient's behalf without informing the patient of that decision
options.rationale: The primary obligation is on the driver. The doctor advises the patient of their notification duty and only reports directly if the patient continues to drive contrary to advice (jurisdiction-dependent mandatory reporting). (Source: Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive 2022)
source_refs: Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive 2022

options.text: He may continue driving without notification provided he keeps his blood pressure below 140/90 and undergoes an annual electrocardiogram
options.rationale: Cardiovascular monitoring is important on stimulant therapy but is separate from the licensing notification obligation for the underlying ADHD diagnosis. (Source: Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive 2022)
source_refs: Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive 2022

options.text: He is required to notify the state driver licensing authority himself, because untreated or treated ADHD may affect fitness to drive under the Austroads criteria
options.rationale: Under Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive, ADHD is a notifiable condition that may affect driving. The legal obligation to notify rests with the driver, not the doctor. The treating doctor advises about impact and reports if the driver does not notify, per state-based mandatory reporting requirements (varies by jurisdiction). (Source: Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive 2022)
source_refs: Austroads Assessing Fitness to Drive 2022

explanation.summary: ADHD is a notifiable condition under Austroads and the primary obligation to notify rests with the driver, not the doctor. Most adults with well-treated ADHD retain their private licence, sometimes with conditions. Doctors must inform the patient of the notification duty and, in jurisdictions with mandatory reporting, report only if the patient continues to drive contrary to advice.
key_points: Austroads is the AU national standard for medical fitness to drive
Primary notification duty is on the driver; doctor documents advice given
Mandatory doctor reporting varies by state (e.g. NT, SA have mandatory reporting; NSW, VIC discretionary)
explanation.pearls: The two-part rule is easy to forget: it is the diagnosis that is notifiable, not the medication. Well-treated ADHD often keeps its licence.

sources.label: RANZCP Adult ADHD Clinical Practice Guideline

stem:
A 26-year-old woman with a history of schizophrenia is brought to the emergency department by her family after 4 days of progressive immobility. She sits motionless with her right arm held in an awkward flexed posture that she maintains for hours when placed by staff. She has not eaten or drunk voluntarily for 24 hours and has been echolalic when spoken to. She has no fever and no rigidity, and she does not resist passive movement of her limbs.

Her regular olanzapine 10 mg nightly has been unchanged for 12 months. She has no illicit drug use per her family and her urine drug screen is negative. Blood tests including full blood count, urea and electrolytes, calcium, creatine kinase and inflammatory markers are within normal limits. A non-contrast computed tomography scan of the brain is normal. Her creatinine is 62 micromol/L (45-90).

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 88, blood pressure 118/72, respiratory rate 16, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees
data_table.Investigations: creatine kinase 90 U/L (less than 200), electrolytes and calcium within normal limits, non-contrast CT brain reported as normal, urine drug screen negative
data_table.Bush-Francis catatonia rating scale: screening positive with mutism, immobility, waxy flexibility, posturing, echolalia

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial diagnostic and therapeutic step?

options.text: Administer intravenous lorazepam 2 mg and observe for improvement in mutism and posturing over the following 15 to 30 minutes as a test
options.rationale: The lorazepam challenge (typically 1 to 2 mg IV) is both diagnostic and therapeutic in catatonia: at least 50 percent improvement in Bush-Francis scale features supports the diagnosis and identifies responders who benefit from a lorazepam trial as ongoing treatment. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Catatonia)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Catatonia

options.text: Increase her olanzapine dose to 20 mg nightly on the assumption that the presentation represents worsening psychotic symptoms not otherwise
options.rationale: Increasing antipsychotic dose in unrecognised catatonia risks progression to malignant catatonia and neuroleptic malignant syndrome. It is not the correct step. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Catatonia)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Catatonia

options.text: Commence subcutaneous dantrolene 1 mg/kg for suspected neuroleptic malignant syndrome pending further biochemistry results and observation
options.rationale: NMS presents with hyperthermia, rigidity, and elevated CK; none are present. The clinical picture is catatonia and dantrolene is not the initial step. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Catatonia)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Catatonia

options.text: Arrange urgent electroconvulsive therapy without any pharmacological trial because ECT is the fastest treatment for catatonia in the acute setting
options.rationale: ECT is highly effective and is escalated to when the lorazepam trial fails or catatonia becomes malignant, but a lorazepam challenge precedes ECT in most cases and provides same-day evidence to guide ongoing care. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Catatonia)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Catatonia

options.text: Perform a lumbar puncture and commence intravenous aciclovir for suspected herpes simplex encephalitis after a normal computed tomography scan
options.rationale: There is no fever, no CSF-suggestive features, and no focal neurology; the pretest probability of HSV encephalitis is very low relative to the strong catatonia phenotype. (Source: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Catatonia)
source_refs: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Catatonia

explanation.summary: The lorazepam challenge (1 to 2 mg IV) is the AU first-line diagnostic and therapeutic step for suspected catatonia. Response supports the diagnosis and identifies patients for ongoing lorazepam treatment. Escalating antipsychotic dose in unrecognised catatonia can precipitate malignant catatonia or NMS. ECT is second-line for lorazepam non-responders and first-line for malignant catatonia.
key_points: Bush-Francis features (mutism, posturing, waxy flexibility, echolalia) trigger the diagnostic pathway
Lorazepam 1 to 2 mg IV challenge with response at 15 to 30 minutes
Escalate to ECT if lorazepam trial fails or in malignant catatonia (hyperthermia, autonomic instability)
explanation.pearls: The absence of fever, rigidity and CK elevation separates catatonia from NMS. Both are treated by stopping the offending antipsychotic; catatonia adds lorazepam, NMS adds cooling and dantrolene.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Catatonia

stem:
A 30-year-old woman is brought to a regional emergency department 90 minutes after an intentional overdose of her partner's amitriptyline. She has taken an estimated 40 tablets of 25 mg (approximately 1000 mg total, weight 60 kg). She was found drowsy at home but is now more alert on arrival with a GCS of 13. She has no history of ischaemic heart disease and takes no other regular medications; she has occasional migraine for which she uses paracetamol.

Initial vitals show pulse rate 128 regular, blood pressure 92/56, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees. Her mucous membranes are dry. Her electrocardiogram shows sinus tachycardia at 128 with a rightward terminal R wave in lead aVR and a QRS duration of 130 milliseconds. Serum electrolytes show sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145) and potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0). Serum paracetamol drawn now is 15 mg/L (treatment line 150 mg/L at 4 hours). Bedside blood glucose is 5.2 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 128, blood pressure 92/56, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees
data_table.Investigations: sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), bicarbonate 22 mmol/L (22-30), venous pH 7.34, QRS 130 milliseconds, terminal R wave in aVR positive, paracetamol level 15 mg/L (subtherapeutic)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer intravenous flumazenil 200 microgram to reverse suspected central nervous system depression from the tricyclic overdose in this case
options.rationale: Flumazenil is a benzodiazepine antagonist and has no role in TCA overdose. It risks precipitating seizures in mixed overdoses. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology - Tricyclic antidepressants)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology - Tricyclic antidepressants

options.text: Administer intravenous phenytoin 15 mg/kg loading dose over 30 minutes to reduce the risk of TCA-related generalised tonic-clonic seizures
options.rationale: Phenytoin is contraindicated in TCA toxicity because it worsens sodium channel blockade and is proarrhythmic. Benzodiazepines are the correct anticonvulsant here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology - Tricyclic antidepressants)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology - Tricyclic antidepressants

options.text: Administer intravenous sodium bicarbonate 8.4 percent 1 to 2 mmol/kg bolus and repeat as needed to target a QRS width under 100 milliseconds
options.rationale: In TCA toxicity, sodium bicarbonate is indicated when the QRS is above 100 milliseconds, there is a positive terminal R wave in aVR, ventricular arrhythmia, or hypotension unresponsive to fluid. Doses of 1 to 2 mmol/kg are given as bolus and repeated with the QRS width as the target endpoint. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology - Tricyclic antidepressants)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology - Tricyclic antidepressants

options.text: Administer intravenous physostigmine 2 mg to reverse the anticholinergic component of the overdose and improve mental status quickly
options.rationale: Physostigmine is contraindicated in TCA overdose because of the risk of asystole and seizures. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology - Tricyclic antidepressants)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology - Tricyclic antidepressants

options.text: Administer intravenous procainamide 100 mg over 5 minutes to control tachycardia and reduce the risk of ventricular arrhythmia progression
options.rationale: Class Ia antiarrhythmics worsen TCA sodium channel blockade and are contraindicated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology - Tricyclic antidepressants)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology - Tricyclic antidepressants

explanation.summary: TCA cardiotoxicity manifests as QRS prolongation and a terminal R wave in aVR, reflecting sodium channel blockade. Sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg IV is both alkalinising and sodium-loading, reversing the channel blockade. The dose is titrated to QRS width under 100 milliseconds. Class Ia and Ic antiarrhythmics and phenytoin are contraindicated. Benzodiazepines treat seizures; intubation and lipid emulsion are reserved for refractory instability.
key_points: Bicarbonate indications: QRS over 100 ms, terminal R in aVR, ventricular arrhythmia, hypotension not responsive to fluid
Target QRS under 100 ms and arterial pH 7.50 to 7.55 during boluses
Contraindicated: flumazenil, physostigmine, phenytoin, class Ia/Ic antiarrhythmics
explanation.pearls: The single most sensitive early ECG marker of significant TCA toxicity is the terminal R wave in aVR greater than 3 mm. It appears before the QRS widens beyond 100 ms.

subtopic_detail: Schizoaffective disorder versus bipolar with psychosis
stem:
A 24-year-old man is admitted with a 4-week episode of persecutory delusions (that ASIO is monitoring him), auditory hallucinations of a running commentary, elevated mood, and reduced need for sleep. He has had two prior similar admissions in the past 3 years. Careful longitudinal history taken from him and his father indicates that between admissions he has continued to hear intermittent voices and hold odd persecutory beliefs for approximately 4 to 6 weeks at a time without any prominent mood elevation, depression, or functional impairment beyond a mild degree.

Collateral confirms two prior manic episodes each lasting 3 to 4 weeks, each with prominent psychotic features, with full inter-episode return of mood to euthymia. He has been abstinent from cannabis and other substances for over 12 months, confirmed by urine drug screens. He has no family history of bipolar disorder. His current medication is quetiapine 400 mg nightly, tolerated well.

data_table.Mental state: elevated mood, pressured speech, grandiose and persecutory delusions, third-person auditory hallucinations, no cognitive impairment
data_table.Substance use: abstinent from cannabis and other substances for over 12 months, current urine drug screen negative
data_table.Collateral: between-episode auditory hallucinations and mild persecutory beliefs persist for approximately 4 to 6 weeks after mood settles

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Bipolar I disorder with mood-congruent psychotic features because he has clear manic episodes and psychotic symptoms only during mood episodes
options.rationale: Bipolar I with psychotic features requires psychotic symptoms to be confined to mood episodes. The persistence of voices and persecutory beliefs for 4 to 6 weeks between mood episodes excludes this. (Source: DSM-5-TR)
source_refs: DSM-5-TR

options.text: Schizophrenia because he has active phase symptoms of hallucinations and delusions with residual features between the acute admissions ongoing
options.rationale: Schizophrenia requires either mood symptoms to be absent OR the total duration of any mood episodes to be brief relative to the psychotic illness. His repeated 3 to 4 week manic episodes are prominent, not brief. (Source: DSM-5-TR)
source_refs: DSM-5-TR

options.text: Substance/medication induced psychotic disorder because cannabis has a very high lifetime prevalence in comorbid psychotic disorders in this age group
options.rationale: He has been abstinent for over 12 months with negative urine drug screens and symptoms have persisted, so a substance-induced diagnosis is not appropriate. (Source: DSM-5-TR)
source_refs: DSM-5-TR

options.text: Schizoaffective disorder because psychotic symptoms persist for at least 2 weeks without prominent mood symptoms during the illness course overall
options.rationale: Schizoaffective disorder (DSM-5) requires an uninterrupted illness with a mood episode concurrent with psychotic symptoms, PLUS at least 2 weeks of psychotic symptoms in the absence of a prominent mood episode. This patient's between-episode voices and delusions lasting 4 to 6 weeks meet this criterion. (Source: DSM-5-TR)
source_refs: DSM-5-TR

options.text: Brief psychotic disorder because his episodes each last less than a month and have a spontaneous resolution back to a functioning premorbid level
options.rationale: Brief psychotic disorder requires symptoms lasting more than a day but less than a month, with full return to premorbid function. His episodes exceed a month and psychotic symptoms persist between them. (Source: DSM-5-TR)
source_refs: DSM-5-TR

explanation.summary: The key discriminator between bipolar I with psychotic features and schizoaffective disorder is whether psychotic symptoms occur ONLY during mood episodes (bipolar I) or persist for at least 2 weeks in the absence of a prominent mood episode (schizoaffective). This patient's 4 to 6 weeks of between-episode auditory hallucinations and persecutory beliefs meet the schizoaffective criterion. Schizophrenia is excluded because mood episodes are not brief relative to the overall course.
key_points: Schizoaffective disorder requires greater than 2 weeks of psychotic symptoms without prominent mood symptoms during the illness course
Bipolar I with psychotic features restricts psychotic symptoms to mood episodes only
Schizophrenia allows brief mood symptoms only, not prominent recurrent manic episodes
explanation.pearls: Nail the schizoaffective diagnosis on the between-episode window. Anything under 2 weeks of psychotic symptoms without mood makes it bipolar with psychotic features; anything longer makes it schizoaffective.

sources.label: RANZCP Clinical Practice Guideline for Schizophrenia and Related Disorders

stem:
A 58-year-old man presents to a metropolitan emergency department with 3 weeks of low-grade fever, weight loss of 4 kg, and increasing dyspnoea on exertion. He had a bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement 2 years ago for calcific aortic stenosis and is otherwise well. He denies any recent dental procedure but had a dental cleaning 6 weeks ago and did not receive antibiotic prophylaxis.

On examination he has a soft early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge and a small linear haemorrhage under his right great toenail. Splinter haemorrhages are visible on his left index finger. Three sets of blood cultures drawn 12 hours apart have all grown Streptococcus sanguinis, sensitive to benzylpenicillin. A transoesophageal echocardiogram today demonstrates a 6 mm mobile echogenic mass on the aortic side of the prosthetic aortic valve with new mild aortic regurgitation.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 96, blood pressure 110/58, respiratory rate 20, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temperature 38.2 degrees
data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 108 g/L (130-180), white cell count 14 x10 to the 9 per litre (4.0-11.0), CRP 82 mg/L (less than 5), creatinine 92 micromol/L (60-110)
data_table.Blood cultures: three sets over 24 hours all positive for Streptococcus sanguinis
data_table.Echocardiography: 6 mm mobile mass on aortic side of prosthetic aortic valve, new mild aortic regurgitation

lead_in: Which of the following statements correctly categorises the modified Duke criteria met by this presentation?

options.text: This meets 1 major and 2 minor criteria only, which is insufficient for a definite diagnosis and requires a possible endocarditis classification while further criteria are sought
options.rationale: The echocardiographic vegetation with new regurgitation on a prosthetic valve is a separate MAJOR criterion, not a minor. Two majors are present. (Source: ESC 2023 Guidelines for Endocarditis, adopted by CSANZ)
source_refs: ESC 2023 Guidelines for Endocarditis, adopted by CSANZ

options.text: This meets 1 major and 4 minor criteria, which meets a definite endocarditis classification and requires no additional echocardiographic imaging at all
options.rationale: There are not 4 minor criteria here (fever above 38 is one minor, splinter haemorrhages are one minor); more importantly the echocardiographic evidence is major and completes a 2-major definite diagnosis. (Source: ESC 2023 Guidelines for Endocarditis, adopted by CSANZ)
source_refs: ESC 2023 Guidelines for Endocarditis, adopted by CSANZ

options.text: This meets 5 minor criteria and no major criteria, allowing a definite endocarditis diagnosis to be made once further blood culture sets are drawn to confirm
options.rationale: Persistent bacteraemia with typical organism and echocardiographic vegetation are both majors, not minors. This case is diagnosed on 2 majors. (Source: ESC 2023 Guidelines for Endocarditis, adopted by CSANZ)
source_refs: ESC 2023 Guidelines for Endocarditis, adopted by CSANZ

options.text: This meets neither major nor sufficient minor criteria and requires cardiac magnetic resonance imaging today before a definite classification can be applied
options.rationale: Two majors are clearly present. Cardiac MRI is an adjunct in problem cases but is not required to make the diagnosis here. (Source: ESC 2023 Guidelines for Endocarditis, adopted by CSANZ)
source_refs: ESC 2023 Guidelines for Endocarditis, adopted by CSANZ

options.text: This meets 2 major criteria (typical organism on persistently positive blood cultures plus echocardiographic vegetation with new regurgitation), sufficient for a definite endocarditis diagnosis
options.rationale: Modified Duke definite endocarditis requires either 2 majors, or 1 major plus 3 minors, or 5 minors. Here the typical organism from persistently positive blood cultures satisfies one major, and the echocardiographic vegetation plus new regurgitation satisfies the second. (Source: ESC 2023 Guidelines for Endocarditis, adopted by CSANZ)
source_refs: ESC 2023 Guidelines for Endocarditis, adopted by CSANZ

explanation.summary: The modified Duke criteria establish definite endocarditis with 2 majors, 1 major plus 3 minors, or 5 minors. Typical organism from persistently positive blood cultures is one major; echocardiographic vegetation with new valvular regurgitation is a second. This patient meets both, warranting a definite diagnosis and immediate treatment planning with cardiology and cardiac surgery input given the prosthetic valve.
key_points: Major criteria: typical organism in 2 or more separate blood cultures; echocardiographic evidence (vegetation, abscess, new prosthetic dehiscence, new regurgitation)
Minor criteria: predisposing condition, fever above 38, vascular phenomena (splinters, Janeway), immunologic (Osler, Roth), microbiological non-major
Prosthetic valve endocarditis requires early cardiac surgery review
explanation.pearls: The trap is calling splinter haemorrhages a major. They are a minor vascular phenomenon. Echocardiographic vegetation is the major.

sources.label: ESC 2023 Guidelines for Endocarditis, adopted by CSANZ

subtopic_detail: COPD GOLD Group E escalation therapy
stem:
A 68-year-old man with a 40 pack-year smoking history and moderate COPD attends his general practice for review after a hospital admission for infective exacerbation 4 weeks ago requiring intravenous antibiotics. This is his second exacerbation this year, the first being managed in the community with oral prednisolone and doxycycline. Spirometry shows post-bronchodilator FEV1 of 55 percent predicted with a modified Medical Research Council dyspnoea score of 2 out of 4.

He stopped smoking during the last admission and has re-engaged with pulmonary rehabilitation. His current inhaled therapy is tiotropium 18 microgram once daily via HandiHaler alone. He reports good adherence and correct inhaler technique demonstrated at the pharmacy. His eosinophil count on the recent admission was 320 cells per microlitre (150-500) and he has no history of asthma or atopic disease.

data_table.Investigations: post-bronchodilator FEV1 55 percent predicted, mMRC 2 out of 4, peripheral eosinophil count 320 cells per microlitre
data_table.Exacerbation history: one community-managed exacerbation and one hospitalisation in the past 12 months

lead_in: What is the most appropriate change to his inhaled therapy?

options.text: Switch tiotropium to a fixed dose LABA plus LAMA (long-acting beta-agonist plus long-acting muscarinic antagonist) combination inhaler in a single device
options.rationale: For GOLD Group E COPD (2 or more moderate exacerbations or 1 hospitalisation in the past year), GOLD 2023 recommends escalating from LAMA monotherapy to LABA plus LAMA. Triple therapy (LABA plus LAMA plus ICS) is added if exacerbations persist AND eosinophils are at or above 300. His eosinophil count is 320 but the initial escalation is dual bronchodilator. (Source: GOLD 2023 COPD Report; Lung Foundation Australia COPD-X)
source_refs: Lung Foundation Australia COPD-X Concise Guide

options.text: Continue tiotropium monotherapy and add a short-acting beta-agonist reliever only, with review in 3 months and repeat spirometry at that time
options.rationale: Group E COPD requires escalation of maintenance therapy, not continuation of monotherapy. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia COPD-X Concise Guide)
source_refs: Lung Foundation Australia COPD-X Concise Guide

options.text: Switch immediately to triple therapy (LABA plus LAMA plus inhaled corticosteroid) as a single combination inhaler on the basis of the elevated eosinophil count
options.rationale: Triple therapy is indicated for Group E patients with continued exacerbations on LABA plus LAMA and eosinophils at or above 300. Jumping straight to triple therapy skips the intermediate step. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia COPD-X Concise Guide)
source_refs: Lung Foundation Australia COPD-X Concise Guide

options.text: Add oral theophylline modified release 200 mg twice daily for its anti-inflammatory effect and repeat serum drug levels at 2 weeks after initiation
options.rationale: Theophylline is a last-resort option due to its narrow therapeutic index and drug interactions and is not recommended before dual bronchodilator escalation. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia COPD-X Concise Guide)
source_refs: Lung Foundation Australia COPD-X Concise Guide

options.text: Commence long term oral prednisolone 5 mg daily to reduce the risk of further exacerbations over the next 12 months of maintenance treatment
options.rationale: Chronic oral corticosteroid therapy is not recommended for stable COPD outside end-stage disease due to systemic toxicity without exacerbation benefit. (Source: Lung Foundation Australia COPD-X Concise Guide)
source_refs: Lung Foundation Australia COPD-X Concise Guide

explanation.summary: GOLD Group E (2 or more moderate exacerbations or 1 hospitalisation in the past year) requires escalation from LAMA monotherapy to LABA plus LAMA. Triple therapy is reserved for patients with continued exacerbations on dual bronchodilator AND eosinophils at or above 300. Non-pharmacological measures (pulmonary rehab, smoking cessation, vaccination) run in parallel.
key_points: Group E: 2 or more moderate exacerbations OR 1 hospitalisation in the past year
Escalate LAMA to LABA plus LAMA first; add ICS only if continued exacerbations and eosinophils at or above 300
COPD-X aligns with GOLD 2023 in Australia
explanation.pearls: Do not skip to triple therapy in a patient with only one prior hospitalisation. Dual bronchodilator is the correct next step; add ICS only if that fails and eosinophils support it.

sources.label: Lung Foundation Australia COPD-X Concise Guide
